clinicalPearls: Early appearance of adrenal androgen-dependent features such as pubic or axillary hair, adult-type body odour, and mild acne before the usual age, without activation of the gonadal axis
Breast development in girls and testicular enlargement in boys are absent, distinguishing it from true (central) precocious puberty
It reflects premature maturation of the adrenal zona reticularis with a rise in adrenal androgens, particularly dehydroepiandrosterone sulphate (DHEAS)
Bone age and growth velocity are usually normal or only mildly advanced, and adult height is generally unaffected
It is largely benign, but marked or rapidly progressive virilisation should prompt exclusion of non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia and androgen-secreting tumours
Premature adrenarche is associated in some children with insulin resistance and a later tendency to polycystic ovary syndrome, warranting attention to metabolic risk
Management is generally reassurance and observation once serious pathology has been excluded
reference.pathophysiology: Adrenarche is the maturation of the adrenal zona reticularis and the associated increase in adrenal androgen secretion (especially DHEAS) that normally precedes gonadal puberty. In premature adrenarche this process begins early, producing androgen-dependent signs such as sexual hair and body odour while the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis remains quiescent, so gonadal maturation does not occur. The adrenal androgens are relatively weak and produced in modest amounts, which is why bone maturation and growth are usually little affected. The trigger for early adrenal maturation is incompletely understood but is linked in some children to insulin resistance and higher body weight, factors that also connect premature adrenarche with later polycystic ovary syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Central precocious puberty with concurrent pubarche
additionalInvestigations: Serum DHEAS and other adrenal androgens (androstenedione, testosterone) appropriate to the degree of virilisation
17-hydroxyprogesterone, with an ACTH stimulation test if non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia is suspected
Bone-age radiograph to assess skeletal maturation
Basal LH and FSH to confirm the gonadal axis is not activated
Adrenal and pelvic imaging if an androgen-secreting tumour is a concern
Metabolic assessment (glucose and insulin indices) where insulin resistance is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly progressive virilisation, clitoromegaly, or a markedly deepened voice suggesting a tumour or significant enzyme defect
Very high androgen levels out of keeping with benign adrenarche
Substantial bone-age advancement or a growth spurt indicating true precocious puberty or excess androgen
An adrenal or pelvic mass on examination or imaging
reference.prognosis: Isolated premature adrenarche is usually benign with a normal adult height and pubertal course; the principal longer-term consideration is an increased risk of insulin resistance and polycystic ovary syndrome in a subset of girls, which merits metabolic awareness.
pitfalls: Assuming benign adrenarche without excluding non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia in more marked cases
Missing an androgen-secreting adrenal or gonadal tumour presenting with rapid virilisation
Confusing premature adrenarche with central precocious puberty, which involves gonadal activation
Neglecting the associated metabolic and later reproductive (PCOS) risks
Over-investigating mild, slowly progressive, isolated pubic hair development
management: Reassurance and observation, as isolated premature adrenarche is a benign normal variant needing no specific hormonal treatment
Exclude non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia and androgen-secreting tumours when virilisation is marked or rapidly progressive
Serial monitoring of growth velocity, bone age and pubertal staging to confirm the benign, non-progressive course
Attention to metabolic risk with weight management and healthy-lifestyle advice, given the association with insulin resistance
Longer-term awareness of, and screening for, polycystic ovary syndrome in susceptible girls
Referral to paediatric endocrinology if features become progressive, virilising or atypical
